fits: Video calls with grandparents and family far away, with a parent holding the phone.
Music, lullabies and scripture stories played aloud while you hold them.
A parent's phone camera, to keep the memories.
bless: Let them see grandma's face and hear her voice every week.
Sing the same lullaby every night; it becomes home to them.
ages.label: Babies and toddlers
rules: No screen time except video chat with family (American Academy of Pediatrics).
No screens in the room where they sleep.
Never a screen to stop crying; hold them instead.
watch: A baby who stops looking up at faces, or whose words come late, when screens are on a lot.
Background television: it cuts the number of words a baby hears from you.
ages.growing: Attachment, trust, first words and walking. A baby learns language from a face that answers back, not from a screen; this is the age when the brain wires itself fastest around real people.

fits: Picture books and scripture stories on a screen, read together, the way you would read a book.
Drawing and building apps, for short spells, beside you.
bless: Record a message or a song for someone who is sick or far away.
Make a card on the tablet and print it for a neighbor.
ages.label: Little ones
rules: About an hour a day at most, of good content, watched with a parent (American Academy of Pediatrics); the WHO says an hour or less for this age too.
No screens at meals, in the car for short trips, or in the hour before bed.
You choose the content; autoplay is off; no 'kids' video feeds unwatched.
watch: Tantrums when the screen goes off, and asking for it first thing in the morning.
Fast, flashing cartoons; they train a short attention span.
Advertisements aimed at them; explain what an ad is.
ages.growing: Imagination, language, self-control, and the first sense of right and wrong. They copy everything, cannot yet tell a story from an advertisement, and feel a sudden stop like a loss.

fits: Learning apps and reading apps, with the settings you chose.
Family video calls, family movie night, uplifting shows chosen together.
Simple creation: drawing, music, photos of family, a first typed story.
bless: Video-call an older relative and ask them a family-history question; record the answer.
Type a thank-you note to a teacher or a bishop.
ages.label: Early school years
rules: Consistent daily limits, written down as a family media plan; screens live in family rooms, never bedrooms.
No personal smartphone, no social media, no online games with strangers' chat.
Filters on every device, and a parent who can see the history.
watch: Fear from something they saw; ask 'did you see anything that scared you?' often.
Sneaking screens, or lying about time.
Comparing themselves with children on a screen.
ages.growing: Reading, friendship, fairness, and a conscience that can be taught. They believe what they see. They want to belong, and they still tell you everything if you make it safe to.

fits: A basic phone or a watch that calls and texts, only if the family truly needs it; a smartphone can wait.
Homework online in a family room, with filters and history visible.
Creating: coding, music, film-making, photography, with the results shared inside the family.
bless: Teach a younger sibling something on the tablet.
Help a grandparent with their phone; that is service too.
Make a family video for a birthday or a farewell.
ages.label: Tweens
rules: No social media (the law sets 13 as the floor; the Surgeon General warns it is not proof of safety).
No devices in bedrooms overnight; they charge in the kitchen.
A family rule that a secret online is never kept from parents, and that closing a bad page and telling is always the right move, never punished.
watch: Withdrawal, secrecy, a phone that is always face-down.
Sleep loss, and mood that tracks the screen.
Anyone online who wants to move the talk to a private app.
ages.growing: Identity, puberty, and the pull of friends. Curiosity is strong and the brakes are not built yet: the part of the brain that weighs consequences finishes growing in the mid-twenties. Most children first meet pornography by accident at about this age, so the talk comes before the device.

fits: A smartphone with a written family agreement, filters, and a parent who knows every account and password.
Tools to create and serve: editing, design, coding, music, a family history project.
Scripture and hymn apps, and talks they choose to listen to.
bless: Share a testimony, a scripture or a kindness online on purpose, not by accident.
Organize a service project with friends through the group chat.
Record grandparents' stories and put them on the family timeline.
ages.label: Young teens
rules: Delay social media as long as you can; if it is used, accounts are private, parents follow, notifications are off, and there is a daily limit.
Phones out of bedrooms at night and off the table at meals; the Surgeon General links heavy use to anxiety, depression and lost sleep.
Talk plainly about pornography, sextortion, bullying and AI 'companions' before they meet them; agree what they will do when they do.
watch: Three hours a day or more on social media doubles the risk of anxiety and depression symptoms (Surgeon General, 2023).
A sudden new 'friend' who sends gifts or asks for pictures.
Comparing their body or their life to a feed.
ages.growing: Abstract thinking, the need to be their own person, and a hunger for approval that social media is built to exploit. Risk feels smaller than it is. Faith becomes their own here, or does not.

fits: Their own limits, written by them and reviewed with you.
AI, design, code and media as tools for real work and real service.
Teaching the younger ones what they have learned.
bless: Lead the family history work; build the family's timeline.
Create something that lifts: music, a short film, a page that helps someone.
Use the tools the way the Lord's work uses them: to reach, to teach, to gather.
ages.label: Older teens
rules: A weekly screen sabbath, and phones away when people are present.
Learn to tell truth from propaganda: check who made it, who paid for it, and what it wants you to feel.
Keep the standards in For the Strength of Youth as their own, not yours.
watch: Driving with a phone in hand.
Gambling built into games and apps.
Letting an AI do the thinking, or the feeling.
ages.growing: Preparing to govern themselves: college, missions, work, marriage. The rules now move from yours to theirs, one at a time, while they are still home to talk about it.

bad: Burning what belongs to other people.
Using it carelessly so it spreads.
Hurting animals or land with it on purpose.
items.why: Fire is the first light people could hold. It gathered families around it at night - the first bedtime circle. Cooked food helped people grow strong and think clearly, ready one day to hear and understand the word of God.

ages.0-2: Never within reach. 'Hot' is one of the first words worth teaching.
ages.16+: Teach the younger ones fire safety; carry the responsibility.
ages.3-5: Watch a campfire from a parent's arms; learn that fire is a helper only when a grown-up holds it.
ages.6-9: Help gather wood and feed a campfire with a grown-up right beside them.
ages.10-12: Light a candle or a stove with permission, and learn how to put a fire out.
ages.13-15: Build, tend and fully put out a campfire; cook a meal on it.

good: Cooking food so it is safe and good to eat.
Keeping a family warm and together on a cold night.
Light to read and talk by after the sun goes down.
harm: Burns and house fires: fire does not know a child from a log.
A fascination with flames that grows if it is a secret.
kids: Only grown-ups light it.
Never leave a fire alone.
Fire is for warming and cooking, never for showing off.
items.name: Fire
items.talk: Fire can cook our dinner or burn our house. What makes the difference?
items.what: People learned to keep a fire and to make one. Warmth, light in the dark, cooked food, and a safe place to gather.
avoid: Matches, lighters and candles left where small hands reach.
Fireworks in a child's hands.
Playing near a stove, a campfire or a heater.
bless: Cook a meal for a family that needs one.
A campfire family night, with stories of the pioneers who cooked over one every night.
Bring warmth to someone: soup, a blanket, a lit porch.
dangers: A fire nobody watches grows fast.
Smoke in a closed room can hurt you.
A wildfire can take homes in an hour.

learned.note: The story never changes: fire blesses the careful and hurts the careless. That is the pattern every later technology follows.

bad: War chariots were one of its first uses.
Rushing so fast that people get hurt.
items.why: The wheel let people carry more than their arms could hold. Food reached hungry cities, families moved to new lands, and one day the wheel would carry scriptures and missionaries across the world.

ages.0-2: Strollers and wagons pulled by a parent.
ages.16+: Driving: the biggest wheel of all, phone out of reach, every time.
ages.3-5: A tricycle or balance bike, helmet on every time.
ages.6-9: A bike on sidewalks and paths with a grown-up near.
ages.10-12: Rides to a friend's house with agreed routes and times.
ages.13-15: Longer rides; learn the road rules a driver keeps.

good: Carrying food and water to people who need it.
Helping a family travel to be together.
Every machine that helps people work: a mill, a bicycle, a car.
harm: Falls, and roads: the wheel goes faster than a child can judge.
A car treated as a toy or a place to play.
kids: Look both ways.
A cart is for carrying, not for racing.
Help load it for someone who cannot.
items.name: The Wheel
items.talk: What do we carry to other people that they could not get on their own?
items.what: A round thing that rolls. Carts, then chariots, then every machine that turns.
avoid: Riding without a helmet.
Streets without a grown-up until they have earned it.
A driver's seat before the law and the family say so.
bless: Deliver a meal or a note on a bike.
Pull a wagon of groceries for a neighbor.
Learn to fix a bike, then fix someone else's.
dangers: Anything that rolls fast can run someone over.
Machines that turn can catch fingers and clothing.

learned.note: The wheel appears in Mesopotamia on pottery first and carts soon after. Its best use was never the chariot; it was bringing food home.

bad: Writing lies about someone.
Writing cruel words that stay and hurt again and again.
Writing to trick people out of what is theirs.
items.why: Without writing there is no scripture. Writing is how Heavenly Father's words reached us across thousands of years, and how your family's stories will reach your grandchildren.

ages.0-2: Scribbles beside you; they learn that marks mean something.
ages.16+: Write the family's stories down; that is family history.
ages.3-5: Their own name, and letters they dictate to you.
ages.6-9: Thank-you notes and a first journal with pictures.
ages.10-12: A real journal, written weekly; letters that get a reply.
ages.13-15: Essays and, above all, a written testimony of their own.

good: Keeping the scriptures so every family can read them.
Writing a letter to someone who is sad.
Writing down what a child said so it is never lost.
harm: Hurtful words on a page or a screen last long after the anger is gone.
Written lies look like truth; children believe what is written down.
kids: Write only what you would say to someone's face.
Write true things.
Write something kind to someone every week.
items.name: Writing
items.talk: If you could write one true thing for your grandchildren to read, what would it be?
items.what: Marks that hold words. Once people could write, a thought could outlive the person who had it.
avoid: Writing anything you would not say to the person's face.
Sharing another person's secret in writing.
Copying someone else's words and calling them your own.
bless: Thank-you notes to teachers, leaders and grandparents.
A journal: the story of their life, kept for their own children.
Letters to a missionary, a soldier, or someone alone.
dangers: Written words can be copied and spread before they are checked.
A lie written well can look like truth.

learned.note: Every screen technology since is still writing: texts, posts and chat are words that stay. A child who learns 'written words last' is ready for all of them.

bad: Printing and passing around things that harm people.
Wasting it: paper is trees.
items.why: Paper made scripture light enough to carry and cheap enough to share. Every book on your shelf, including the bedtime books, stands on this Chinese invention.

ages.0-2: Board books; let them turn the pages.
ages.16+: Keep a paper journal for the things too sacred for a screen.
ages.3-5: Crayons and paper every day; a picture for grandma.
ages.6-9: Their own books, and a shelf to keep them on.
ages.10-12: Paper scriptures of their own, marked in their own hand.
ages.13-15: Study on paper as well as on a screen; it sticks better.

good: Books a family can afford.
Drawing and letters for someone who is far away.
Keeping records so that promises are kept.
harm: Very little. Paper is one of the safest gifts a child can be handed.
kids: Treat books gently; they are someone's work.
Use both sides.
A hand-written note is a gift.
items.name: Paper
items.talk: Why do we still love paper books when we have screens?
items.what: Thin sheets made from plant fibre. Cheap enough that ordinary people could own writing.
avoid: Tearing and wasting; teach that paper is a tree and a gift.
Reading only screens: paper rests the eyes and settles the mind.
bless: Handmade cards for the lonely.
A scrapbook of the family's year.
Wrap a gift with your own drawing on it.
dangers: Paper burns and rots; things kept only on paper can be lost.
Cheap copies made false ideas easy to spread too.

learned.note: Reading on paper still helps children remember more than reading the same words on a screen, in study after study. That is why the bedtime books are printed.

bad: Printing lies faster than anyone can answer them.
Printing things that make people cruel or ashamed.
items.why: Before the press, a Bible cost more than a house. After it, ordinary families could read the scriptures in their own homes. A boy reading his own Bible in his own home is how the Restoration began.

ages.0-2: Board books, read aloud every day.
ages.16+: Publish something of their own; the press is theirs too.
ages.3-5: Picture books at bedtime, the same ones over and over; that is how they learn.
ages.6-9: Their own library card, books chosen together.
ages.10-12: Chapter books, and the first lesson in checking a claim: who wrote this, and how do they know?
ages.13-15: Read widely, the classics included, and learn to spot propaganda by its feel.

good: Scriptures in every home, in every language.
Books that teach children to read.
News that tells the truth to everyone at once.
harm: Printed lies look true; propaganda was printed on the same presses as scripture.
Books and magazines carry adult content into a home as easily as good words.
kids: Ask who wrote it and why.
Read the scriptures for yourself.
Just because it is printed does not make it true.
items.name: The Printing Press
items.talk: What would it be like if only one family in town owned a Bible?
items.what: A machine that presses inked letters onto paper, page after page. The first big book it printed was the Bible.
avoid: Books and magazines a parent has not looked at first.
Believing something because it is in print.
Comics and fan stories from unknown sources.
bless: Print a family book of your own stories.
Give scriptures to someone who has none.
Make a neighborhood newsletter that tells the good news.
dangers: Whoever owns the press decides what millions read.
Propaganda - printed lies - has started wars.

learned.note: Within fifty years of the press there were eight million books in Europe. Fifty years after the smartphone there are five billion of them. Both changed everything, faster than anyone planned for.

bad: Spying on people who want to be left alone.
Aiming weapons from far away.
items.why: The heavens declare the glory of God, and the telescope let us read that declaration. The same glass, turned the other way, became the microscope and showed the tiny worlds that keep us alive.

ages.16+: Teach a younger child the sky.
ages.3-5: The moon and the bright planets through binoculars on a parent's lap.
ages.6-9: A small telescope with a grown-up; learn the moon's face.
ages.10-12: Find Jupiter's moons the way Galileo did.
ages.13-15: Learn the constellations and how far the light has come.

good: Learning how big and orderly Heavenly Father's creation is.
Finding ships in trouble at sea.
Microscopes that find sickness so doctors can heal it.
harm: Only one: never point it at the sun.
kids: Look up at night; wonder is a gift.
Use it to learn, not to spy.
Share what you see.
items.name: The Telescope
items.talk: When you look at the stars, what do you think Heavenly Father wants you to feel?
items.what: Curved glass that brings far things close. Galileo pointed one at the sky and saw moons around Jupiter.
avoid: Looking at the sun through any lens.
Buying a toy telescope that shows nothing; a good pair of binoculars is better.
bless: Show a friend the moon's craters for the first time.
Let wonder turn into gratitude: 'the heavens declare the glory of God.'
Star-gaze with the family on a clear night and read Abraham 3 or Psalm 8.
dangers: Never look at the sun through one; it can blind you in a second.

learned.note: Every telescope since Galileo has found more order, not less. The sky is still the easiest place to feel small and loved at the same time.

bad: Factories that worked small children twelve hours a day.
Smoke that made whole cities sick.
items.why: Steam shrank the world. Missionaries crossed oceans in weeks instead of months, and the Saints crossed a continent to gather. Work that broke backs could be done by a machine, so children could go to school.

ages.16+: Repair and build; machines as a way to serve.
ages.3-5: Toy engines and a museum visit.
ages.6-9: Take a simple machine apart with a grown-up.
ages.10-12: Help with tools, with safety glasses and supervision.
ages.13-15: Learn a power tool properly, from a parent.

good: Trains that bring families together across a country.
Pumping clean water into cities.
Factories that make warm clothes cheap enough for everyone.
harm: Machines do not stop for a hand or a foot.
kids: Machines should make people's lives better, not people smaller.
Rest is not laziness.
Thank the people who keep the engines running.
items.name: The Steam Engine
items.talk: If a machine could do your chores, what would you do with the time?
items.what: Boiling water pushes a piston, and the piston turns a wheel. Trains, ships and factories that never got tired.
avoid: Playing near running machinery or engines.
Treating a lawn mower or a power tool as a toy.
bless: Learn how a machine works, then fix one for someone who cannot.
Mow, plow or haul for a neighbor with the machine you have.
dangers: A boiler that is not watched can explode.
When machines do the work, people can be treated like machines.

learned.note: It took laws, not machines, to get children out of the factories. A new tool does not decide how it is used; people do.

bad: Pictures taken to embarrass or shame someone.
Pictures that show what should stay private.
Faked pictures that tell lies.
items.why: A photograph lets a child see the great-grandmother who prayed for them. Family history became something you could hold. Every face in your scrapbook is here because of this.

ages.0-2: Parents take the photos and keep them private.
ages.16+: Become the family's photographer and historian.
ages.3-5: Hold the family camera with a parent; photos stay in the family.
ages.6-9: A simple camera of their own; nothing shared online.
ages.10-12: No camera phone in a bedroom; ask before sharing any picture of a person.
ages.13-15: The rule that never bends: no photo of your body to anyone, and no photo kept secret from parents.

good: Remembering the people we love, exactly as they were.
Showing the truth of something that happened far away.
A picture for someone who cannot be there.
harm: A photo shared can never be taken back; it can be copied, changed and used against them.
Constant comparison with edited pictures of other people's lives.
Predators ask for pictures first.
kids: Ask before you take someone's picture.
Never share a picture that would embarrass someone.
If a picture makes you feel yucky, tell a grown-up.
items.name: Photography
items.talk: Which photograph in our house means the most to you, and why?
items.what: Light on a treated plate makes a picture of exactly what was there. For the first time a face could be kept.
avoid: Sharing a photo of a friend without asking them.
Any photo in a bathroom, bedroom or swimsuit sent to anyone.
Sending a picture to someone you have not met in person.
bless: Photograph the family's history: grandparents, homes, headstones, hands.
Send pictures to a grandparent every Sunday.
Take the pictures at a service project so the story can be told.
dangers: A photo can be copied forever and shown to anyone.
Some pictures are not meant for children's eyes, and they arrive without warning.

learned.note: Today a phone takes a hundred pictures where a plate took one. The rule did not change: a picture is a gift when it is kept for love and a weapon when it is used for shame.

bad: Spreading panic before the facts are known.
Sending orders to hurt people, fast.
items.why: The first message ever sent was a scripture: 'What hath God wrought' (Numbers 23:23). Distance stopped being a wall. Good news, and the gospel, could travel as fast as lightning.

ages.16+: Use the fastest word for the kindest reasons.
ages.3-5: Tap a code on the table: two taps means 'hello'.
ages.6-9: Learn the alphabet in Morse for fun.
ages.10-12: Understand that every text is a telegraph, and every telegraph is read by someone.
ages.13-15: Check a message before you pass it on.

good: Calling for help fast in an emergency.
Telling a family far away that everyone is safe.
Sending truth faster than a rumour can walk.
harm: Rumors travel as fast as truth once messages fly.
kids: Fast is not the same as true.
Wait before you pass something on.
Use it to say 'I am safe' and 'I love you'.
items.name: The Telegraph
items.talk: If you could send one message to anyone in the world right now, who would it be and what would it say?
items.what: Electric pulses down a wire, tapped out as dots and dashes. A message across a country in a minute instead of a month.
avoid: Passing on a message you have not checked.
bless: A quick word of comfort can reach across the world in a second; send one.
Learn Morse code together; tap out 'I love you.'
dangers: The faster news moves, the less time anyone has to check it.
Whoever controls the wire controls what people hear.

learned.note: The telegraph made the first 'breaking news'. People in 1850 complained that it made them anxious and hurried. It is not a new feeling.

bad: Calls that scare or trick people, especially the elderly.
Talking on it while you should be with the people in front of you.
items.why: A grandmother's voice at bedtime from a thousand miles away. A prophet's voice reaching every home at once. The telephone gave families a way to stay close when life spread them out.

ages.0-2: Video calls so family faces stay familiar.
ages.16+: Their phone, their manners, their calls of service.
ages.3-5: Talk to grandma on speaker with you.
ages.6-9: Use the family phone with permission; learn to answer politely.
ages.10-12: A basic phone that calls and texts, only if truly needed, and only known numbers.
ages.13-15: Call etiquette; never answer or call strangers; the phone sleeps outside the bedroom.

good: Hearing the voice of someone you miss.
Calling a doctor or the fire department fast.
Checking on a neighbour who lives alone.
harm: Strangers can call a child; scammers call everyone.
Late-night calls steal sleep and privacy.
kids: Never give your name or address to a caller you do not know.
Put it down when someone is talking to you.
Call Grandma.
items.name: The Telephone
items.talk: Whose voice would you most like to hear tonight?
items.what: A voice turned into electricity and back into a voice. For the first time you could hear someone who was not in the room.
avoid: Giving a name, an address or a family's plans to any caller.
Answering unknown numbers alone.
Calls after the family's bedtime.
bless: Call grandparents every week; it is the call they wait for.
Check on a lonely neighbor or a widow by phone.
Be the one who calls to say sorry.
dangers: Anyone can call a child; not everyone who calls is a friend.
A phone can interrupt every meal and every bedtime if you let it.

learned.note: Phone scams now take billions of dollars a year, mostly from older people. Teaching grandparents 'hang up and call back' is a real act of love.

bad: Lights that never go off, so nobody rests.
Bright screens and lights in the bedroom that keep children awake.
items.why: Light is the oldest sign of Heavenly Father's work: 'Let there be light.' Electric light let families read, study and gather after the sun went down, safely, and it lit the hospitals and schools that followed.

ages.16+: Keep their own dark, quiet hour before sleep.
ages.3-5: Lights off means eyes closed; keep the rule kindly.
ages.6-9: A reading lamp and a bedtime, both kept.
ages.10-12: No screens for an hour before bed; the light itself is the problem.
ages.13-15: Learn why blue light steals sleep, then choose.

good: Reading the scriptures together after dark.
Hospitals that can work through the night.
Streets that are safe to walk at night.
harm: Light at night, especially from screens, tells the body it is day; sleep suffers, and so does everything sleep protects.
kids: Lights off when you leave the room.
Dark room, better sleep.
Never touch a plug with wet hands.
items.name: The Electric Light
items.talk: Why do you think the very first thing created was light?
items.what: A glowing wire inside a glass bulb. Night stopped being dark, in every room, at the flip of a switch.
avoid: Bright screens and lights in the bedroom after dark.
Leaving every light on; a child should know light costs something.
bless: A lamp for reading scriptures together at night.
Leave a porch light on for someone coming home late.
Bring a flashlight and a meal to a neighbor whose power is out.
dangers: Electricity can hurt you: water and outlets do not mix.
Too much light at night confuses the body's clock and steals sleep.

learned.note: Children sleep better and longer in a dark room, and the blue light of screens at bedtime pushes sleep later. Dim the lights an hour before bed and the body does the rest.

bad: Hateful voices reaching millions at once.
Selling people things they do not need, all day long.
items.why: For the first time a sermon, a prophet, a hymn could reach every home at the same moment. General Conference, missionary broadcasts and the gospel in a hundred languages all ride on radio.

ages.16+: Curate what fills the house; it shapes everyone in it.
ages.3-5: Children's music and hymns; sing along.
ages.6-9: Audiobooks and scripture stories read aloud.
ages.10-12: Podcasts chosen together and listened to together first.
ages.13-15: Their music, checked against For the Strength of Youth by them, not only by you.

good: Music and stories for a family in the kitchen.
Warnings before a storm reaches you.
Good words reaching people who cannot read.
harm: Words and songs go in without a filter: explicit lyrics, adult talk, endless news.
kids: Ask who is talking and what they want.
Turn it off for dinner.
Sing along to the good stuff.
items.name: Radio
items.talk: If you had a radio show everyone in the world could hear, what would you say?
items.what: Voices and music sent through the air with no wire at all. One person speaks and a whole nation hears.
avoid: Music with explicit lyrics, even if the tune is good.
Talk shows and podcasts made for adults.
Radio or headphones on all day; silence is where thinking happens.
bless: Hymns and scripture audio in the car and the kitchen.
Make a family 'radio show' and send it to grandparents.
A playlist that lifts a friend who is down.
dangers: The first mass propaganda was on radio, and it helped start a world war.
A voice in the room feels like a friend even when it is not.

learned.note: Radio taught the world that a voice reaching millions must be chosen carefully. Every feed and channel since is the same lesson at a larger scale.

bad: Films that make cruelty look fun and sin look free.
Watching so much that there is no time left to live your own story.
items.why: Stories are how Jesus taught. A moving picture can carry a parable into a heart that will not sit still for a sermon. The Church's films, and every good family movie, stand here.

ages.16+: Their own standards, held for their own reasons.
ages.3-5: Short, gentle films with a parent, in the daytime.
ages.6-9: G and PG films chosen together; ask afterwards what they felt.
ages.10-12: PG, with a talk after; PG-13 is a parent's call, case by case.
ages.13-15: PG-13 with your judgment, never R; teach why, not just no.

good: A story the whole family watches and talks about.
Seeing places and people you could never visit.
Films that teach faith and courage.
harm: Images stay: a frightening scene at six is remembered at forty.
Violence and sexual content seen young numb what should stay tender.
Long films replace play, sleep and talk.
kids: Watch with your family, not alone.
If it makes you feel dark, turn it off.
Talk about the story afterwards.
items.name: Movies
items.talk: What is the best movie we have watched together, and what did it teach?
items.what: Pictures shown fast enough that they seem to move. A story you can watch with a crowd.
avoid: Ratings above their age, and PG-13 or R because 'everyone has seen it.'
Horror at any age of childhood.
Watching alone anything a parent has not seen.
bless: Family movie night with a film that lifts, then talk about it.
Make a family movie: a story, a play, a birthday, a farewell.
Watch the Savior's life together and talk about Him.
dangers: What you watch shapes what you want. Choose it like you choose friends.
Some films are made to frighten or excite in ways that stay with a child for years.

learned.note: Children copy what they see on screens more than what they are told. A parent watching beside them, asking 'was that right?', changes what the story teaches.

bad: Leaving it on all day so it raises the children.
Shows that make wrong look normal.
Ads that teach children to want and want.
items.why: Television carried General Conference and the words of prophets into homes that could never travel to hear them. It let a family see the world Heavenly Father made, from the ocean floor to the moon.

ages.0-2: None, except family on a video call.
ages.16+: Decide what deserves an evening.
ages.3-5: About an hour of good programs, with you, never as a babysitter.
ages.6-9: A daily limit that is kept; shows chosen together.
ages.10-12: Shows in the family room; learn what an ad is doing to you.
ages.13-15: Their own choices, measured against the family's standard.

good: Watching the prophet speak, as a family.
Learning about animals, places and history.
A game or a show that brings the family to one couch.
harm: Television on in the background lowers how much parents talk to babies, and how much babies learn to talk.
Hours of passive watching replace play, reading and sleep.
Advertising teaches a child to want.
kids: Ask before you turn it on.
One show, then something real.
No TV in the bedroom.
items.name: Television
items.talk: What would our evenings look like with no TV for a week?
items.what: Movies and radio together, in a box in the living room. The world came into the house.
avoid: A television in a bedroom.
TV on during meals or as background all day.
Channels and streaming feeds that autoplay whatever comes next.
bless: Watch general conference and the Savior's story together.
Uplifting programs the whole family talks about afterwards.
Turn it off and read the story instead, some nights.
dangers: Hours a day in front of it are linked to less reading, less sleep and less play.
The living room stops being for talking.

learned.note: By the 1980s the average American child watched more television than they spent in school. It was the first screen to be blamed for what screens do, and the lessons learned then still hold.

bad: Cheating, stealing and spying, all made faster.
Machines built to keep people playing or scrolling.
items.why: Family history, scripture search, the app you are reading this in: all of it is a computer keeping track of what matters. It was built to think fast so that people could spend their thinking on what only people can do.

ages.16+: A tool for a life's work; they set the limits and keep them.
ages.3-5: Not needed.
ages.6-9: Learning games and typing, in a family room, with limits.
ages.10-12: Homework, coding for fun, a family history project; history visible to parents.
ages.13-15: Real work: writing, design, code, editing; filters stay on.

good: Finding your ancestors in records from around the world.
Helping doctors, farmers and teachers do more good.
Keeping the scriptures searchable in every language.
harm: Hours sitting still, hunched, staring.
A computer in a private room is a private door to the whole world.
kids: A computer is a tool, like a hammer. Use it to build.
Keep your passwords secret, even from friends.
When you are done, get up and go outside.
items.name: The Computer
items.talk: What is one thing a computer can never do that you can?
items.what: A machine that follows instructions, millions of times a second. It counts, sorts, remembers and draws.
avoid: A computer in a bedroom.
Accounts a parent does not know about.
Downloading what a parent has not approved.
bless: Learn to code and build something that helps someone.
Type up grandma's stories and the family's history.
Help index old records so families can find their ancestors.
dangers: What is stored on a computer can be stolen or lost.
A computer will do exactly what it is told, even when the instruction is wrong.

learned.note: The first computers filled rooms and were used to aim guns. Within a lifetime they were used to find grandmothers in old census books. Purpose is chosen, not built in.

bad: Games built to keep you playing and spending, with no end.
Games where hurting people is the fun part.
Strangers in a game chat who are not who they say.
items.why: Play is how children learn. A good game teaches patience, problem-solving and teamwork, and a family that plays together laughs together. Games can be built to teach anything, including scripture.

ages.16+: Their own hours, but the same rule: real people before pixels.
ages.3-5: None, or a few minutes of a simple touch game on a parent's lap.
ages.6-9: E-rated games, together, with a timer everyone can see.
ages.10-12: E10+ games, no online chat, a timer, and weekends more than school nights.
ages.13-15: T-rated with a parent's judgment; chat only with known friends; no loot boxes; no games in bedrooms.

good: Playing together as a family and laughing.
Games that teach maths, reading, music or the scriptures.
Making your own game and learning how things work.
harm: Games are built to keep a child playing: rewards, streaks and loot boxes work on a young brain like slot machines.
Violence rehearsed for hours teaches the hands and dulls the heart.
Chat and voice with strangers; predators go where children play.
kids: Play with people you know.
Set a timer before you start, and stop when it rings.
Never buy anything in a game without asking.
items.name: Video Games
items.talk: What game could we play together this week, and what does it teach?
items.what: A game you play on a screen. Pong, then Mario, then whole worlds.
avoid: Games rated above their age (E is for everyone; T is for teens; M is not for children).
Online chat or voice with anyone the family does not know in person.
Loot boxes and in-game purchases; that is gambling with a costume on.
Playing in a bedroom, or after bedtime.
bless: Play together as a family; a game can be a table everyone sits at.
Creative games: build a temple, a city, a world, and show it off.
Invite a lonely child to play in the same room.
dangers: Some games are designed like slot machines; the 'loot box' is a bet.
Hours disappear; sleep, homework and friends disappear with them.
Online chat inside games is where strangers reach children most.

learned.note: Several countries now treat loot boxes as gambling and limit game time for children. Games with a clear end and games played beside a parent show none of the harms of endless online ones.
A systematic review found that excessive video game play is associated with poorer academic performance and increased behavioral problems in children.
A review by Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that specially designed video games can modestly improve mental health in children and teens with anxiety, depression, and ADHD.

A global study involving over 2.8 million children across 64 countries found that increased screen time, including video games, is linked to poorer academic achievement and language development, as well as higher socioemotional and mental health problems.

A systematic review and meta-analysis revealed that exergaming can promote physical activity and improve cognitive flexibility in children, though its effects on motor skills and other cognitive functions were not statistically significant.

A study of preschool children found that brief digital or traditional gameplay improved performance on tasks requiring quick responses but reduced performance on tasks demanding greater concentration and self-control.

A systematic review and meta-analysis indicated that exergaming has significant effects on glucose and lipid metabolism in children and adolescents, suggesting potential benefits for managing metabolic health.

A scoping review found that video and app-based games could serve as beneficial tools to support youth emotion regulation through various strategies, though some studies reported areas of continued difficulty.

bad: Sitting alone in a room for hours.
Copying other people's work and calling it yours.
items.why: Family history left the archives and came home. A parent could type the family's stories, print a lesson, and keep the records Heavenly Father asked us to keep, in the kitchen.

ages.16+: Their own workstation, their own standards.
ages.3-5: Not needed.
ages.6-9: A family computer in a family room, with a child account.
ages.10-12: Homework and creating; a parent can see everything.
ages.13-15: Real tools, with the filter still on and the door open.

good: Writing the family's history and printing it for the grandchildren.
Learning any skill from your own desk.
Running a small business from home.
harm: The whole world on a desk, good and bad alike, unless a parent shapes it.
kids: Use it where the family can see the screen.
Save your work, then save it again.
Make something with it, not just watch something on it.
items.name: The Personal Computer
items.talk: What could you create on a computer that would bless somebody?
items.what: A computer small and cheap enough to sit on a family's desk.
avoid: A home computer without a filter and a family account.
Private browsing and cleared history.
Free downloads that carry viruses and worse.
bless: Write a book, design a card, make music, edit a family film.
Learn a skill that will one day feed a family.
Help an elderly neighbor with their computer.
dangers: A computer in a child's bedroom is a door with no one watching it.
Files can be lost in a second; keep a copy.

learned.note: The rule that came out of the personal computer years still works best: keep it in a shared room where the screen faces the family.

bad: Pornography reached homes through this door, and it reaches children first.
Lies that spread around the world before the truth has its shoes on.
Strangers who pretend to be friends.
items.why: The gospel to every nation, kindred, tongue and people: the internet is the road that promise travels on. Scriptures in a hundred languages, family history from every country, a prophet's words the moment they are spoken.

ages.16+: Their own filters and habits, built while you were still there to help.
ages.3-5: No browsing; a parent plays the chosen video.
ages.6-9: Filtered, in a family room, on a short list of sites you chose, with a parent beside them.
ages.10-12: Filtered and monitored in family rooms; teach the plan for a bad page: close it, tell a parent, never punished.
ages.13-15: Filters plus accountability; talk often about what they meet; they know you will ask.

good: Scriptures, talks and family records for the whole world, free.
Learning anything from anyone, anywhere.
Finding your family across oceans.
harm: Pornography finds children before they look for it: most first see it by accident, around age twelve, and it teaches lies about love and bodies.
Predators, scams and bullying reach into a bedroom.
Endless information with no way to tell true from false.
kids: If you see something yucky, look away and tell a grown-up. You are not in trouble.
Never tell a stranger where you live or go to school.
Ask before you download anything.
items.name: The Internet and the Web
items.talk: What is the best thing the internet has brought into our home? What is the worst?
items.what: Every computer in the world able to talk to every other one. The web put pages on it that anyone can read.
avoid: Unfiltered browsing anywhere, on any device, including a friend's.
Searching alone before they know what to do with what appears.
Clicking ads, pop-ups and 'free' downloads.
Private browsing modes and cleared histories.
bless: Learn anything: a language, an instrument, how to fix the sink.
Find a scripture, a talk, a hymn in seconds and share it.
Serve: find who needs help, and organize the helpers.
dangers: The average child first sees pornography online around age 12, often by accident.
Everything posted can be copied and kept forever.
A screen with no limits is a river with no banks.

learned.note: Filters and family rules help, but the thing that works most is a parent who talks about it early and often, before something is seen, not after.

A study in the Journal of Development Economics found that early exposure to high-speed internet may negatively impact children's communication and social skills, highlighting the need for mindful internet use.

bad: Texting while driving.
Being with people but not really with them.
items.why: A mother can be called from anywhere. Help can be summoned from a roadside. Missionaries in far places can reach their families. The phone in a pocket was made to keep people safe and close.

ages.0-2: A parent's phone is not a pacifier.
ages.16+: Their phone, with limits they wrote and keep.
ages.3-5: Still not a toy; video calls with family only.
ages.6-9: No phone of their own.
ages.10-12: A basic phone or watch that calls and texts, only if the family truly needs it.
ages.13-15: A smartphone only with a written family agreement, filters, and no bedroom overnight; many families wait until high school.

good: Calling for help wherever you are.
Telling your family you are safe.
A quick 'I love you' in the middle of a day.
harm: A phone that is always there is always pulling.
Texts at night steal sleep; texts from strangers steal safety.
kids: Phones down at the table.
Never text a driver, and never text while riding a bike.
Answer your parents.
items.name: The Mobile Phone
items.talk: When is a phone a helper, and when is it a wall between us?
items.what: A telephone with no wire, small enough to carry. Anyone could be reached anywhere.
avoid: A phone in the bedroom overnight.
Group chats a parent does not know about.
A phone at the table or in the car with the driver.
bless: A text that says 'I'm praying for you' at the right moment.
Call the person, not just the text.
Coordinate service: rides, meals, visits.
dangers: Distracted driving kills thousands a year; a text can wait.
A phone that is always on you means work and worry are always on you too.

learned.note: The mobile phone taught families the phrase 'phones down at dinner'. It is still the single best rule.

Research in BMC Public Health showed that increased screen use in early childhood is associated with shorter sleep duration and more sleep problems, emphasizing the importance of managing screen time.
Research suggests that excessive smartphone use can negatively impact adolescents' cognitive development, leading to decreased attention spans and academic performance.

A study in the U.S. linked excessive screen time in children and adolescents to higher risks of anxiety, depression, behavior problems, and ADHD, with physical activity and sleep as mediating factors.
A meta-analysis revealed that parental device use during parent-child interactions is moderately to largely associated with children's internalizing and externalizing mental health problems.
A systematic review indicated that excessive screen use negatively impacts sleep duration and quality in preschool children, potentially leading to behavioral and cognitive issues.
A meta-analysis found that digital interventions can effectively promote mental health in children and adolescents, suggesting potential benefits of technology when used appropriately.
A recent study found that children who use mobile devices at bedtime are more likely to experience reduced sleep quality and duration, leading to increased daytime sleepiness.
Experts recommend keeping phones and tablets out of children's bedrooms overnight to prevent disrupted sleep and compulsive use.
A study found that excessive screen time in children is associated with mental health issues and ADHD, mediated by reduced physical activity and irregular sleep patterns.

bad: Comparing your real life to everyone else's best moments.
Bullying that follows a child home and into bed.
Feeds built to keep you scrolling long after you wanted to stop.
items.why: At its best it is the ward newsletter for the whole world: families far apart share a birthday, a missionary shares the gospel, a lonely person finds a friend. The good in it is real, and it is why so many wanted it.

ages.16+: Purposeful use with their own limits; a weekly day away from it.
ages.3-5: None.
ages.6-9: None.
ages.10-12: None; the law says 13 and the Surgeon General says even that is not proof of safety.
ages.13-15: Delay it as long as you can. If it is used: private accounts, parents follow and know the passwords, notifications off, a daily limit, nothing in bedrooms.

good: Keeping in touch with family who live far away.
Sharing something good and true with many people at once.
Finding others who believe what you believe.
harm: Built to keep a child scrolling: the feed never ends, and every like is a small reward on a young brain.
Comparison, exclusion, bullying and sextortion happen here; teens who use it three or more hours a day face double the risk of anxiety and depression symptoms (U.S. Surgeon General, 2023).
Sleep loss, and a self-worth that rises and falls with strangers' approval.
kids: No account until you are old enough, and your parents say when.
Never post something you would not want Grandma to see.
If someone is mean to you online, show a grown-up right away.
items.name: Social Media
items.talk: We saw what social media did to a lot of kids before anyone knew. What would you want to know before you got an account?
items.what: Websites and apps where everyone posts and everyone watches. Facebook, then Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and the rest.
avoid: Any account under 13 (that is the law) and, most experts now say, well after.
Secret accounts, second accounts, and direct messages with strangers.
Posting photos of their body, their school, their home or their location.
Endless scrolling; use it for a purpose and put it down.
bless: Share a testimony, a scripture, a kindness, on purpose.
Organize a service project with friends.
Keep a family group where the good news gets told first.
dangers: We did not know, and now we do: heavy use is linked to anxiety, sadness and poor sleep in teens, especially girls.
Apps are designed by experts to be hard to put down.
Strangers, predators and scams reach children here.

learned.note: The U.S. Surgeon General warned in 2023 that social media is not proven safe for children and teens, and several countries have since set minimum ages of 15 or 16. Waiting until at least 16 for a child's own account is now the mainstream advice.
learned.source: Surgeon General advisory, 2023; national age laws, summarised

learned.note: Teen anxiety and depression rose sharply after 2012, the year smartphones and social media reached most teenagers. Many researchers now see that as cause, not coincidence.
Studies indicate that passive engagement with short-form digital media, such as scrolling through social media feeds, is associated with higher levels of anxiety and depression among adolescents.
Research indicates that excessive use of social media platforms can negatively impact adolescents' mental health, contributing to increased anxiety and depression.
learned.source: Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development

learned.note: A global study found that high screen time, including social media use, is linked to lower academic achievement and increased mental health issues in children.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services released an advisory highlighting the risks of excessive screen use among children, linking it to increased anxiety, depression, and developmental challenges.

The National Conference of State Legislatures reported that states are implementing policies to address the mental health impacts of social media and emerging technologies on youth, including AI safeguards and digital literacy efforts.
The American Academy of Pediatrics emphasized that screen time limits alone are insufficient, advocating for a comprehensive approach to digital media use that considers content quality and context.

bad: Looking at it instead of at the people you love.
Endless scrolling that eats evenings.
Taking it to bed.
items.why: The scriptures, the family's photos, a prophet's voice and a way to call for help, all in a pocket. This app lives here. Used with care, it is the most useful tool a family has ever carried.

ages.0-2: A parent's phone, held by the parent, for family video calls; not a toy, not a babysitter.
ages.16+: Their own phone under their own rules, learned while they were home.
ages.3-5: A parent's phone, held by the parent, for family video calls; not a toy, not a babysitter.
ages.6-9: No smartphone.
ages.10-12: No smartphone; a basic phone or a watch if the family needs one.
ages.13-15: Only with a written family agreement, filters, parent-known passwords and no bedroom overnight; many experts say wait until high school.

good: Scriptures and this app anywhere you go.
A camera for every family memory.
Maps, help and family one tap away.
harm: Every other technology on this list in one pocket, always on, always pulling.
A camera, a chat and a browser with a child at bedtime, alone.
Attention broken into pieces; the mind never rests.
kids: It sleeps in the kitchen, not in your room.
People in the room come first.
Use it to make something or reach someone, then put it down.
items.name: The Smartphone
items.talk: Let's each say one thing our phone helps with and one thing it steals.
items.what: A phone, a camera, a computer and the whole internet in one pocket. The iPhone came first; now almost everyone has one.
avoid: A smartphone in a bedroom overnight; it charges in the kitchen.
Apps installed without a parent's approval.
Deleted histories and hidden folders.
The phone at meals, in worship, and while driving.
bless: Scriptures, hymns and talks in a pocket everywhere.
Navigation to someone who needs help; a call to someone alone.
Record the stories of the old and the first words of the young.
dangers: The average person checks it well over a hundred times a day; children learn that from us.
A phone in the bedroom steals about an hour of sleep a night.
It can put every danger of the internet into a child's hand, unwatched.

learned.note: Schools that lock phones away during the day report more talking, more play and better learning. Many countries and states now require it.
Waiting to give a child their own smartphone until high school, and a 'dumb' phone before that, is now common advice from pediatricians.

A review in Frontiers in Psychology found that excessive smartphone use among adolescents is linked to sleep disruption, reduced attention, and increased anxiety, suggesting the need for balanced usage.

bad: Autoplay that turns one video into three hours.
Videos made to shock, scare or sell.
Copying dangerous stunts.
items.why: A gospel talk, a hymn, a how-to for fixing the sink, a lesson from the best teacher in the world: streaming put good teaching within reach of every child. The Travelers' own videos will live here.

ages.16+: Decide what deserves their evenings.
ages.3-5: One short show a day, chosen by you, with you.
ages.6-9: A locked child profile, autoplay off, a daily limit.
ages.10-12: Titles chosen together; teach ratings and why.
ages.13-15: Their choices within the family's standard; talk about what they watch.

good: Learning any skill by watching someone kind explain it.
Watching a talk or a hymn together.
Stories and lessons for children, chosen by parents.
harm: Autoplay never stops; one episode becomes a night.
'Kids' profiles can still surface content no child should see.
Binge watching replaces sleep, play and people.
kids: Autoplay off. You choose the next one, with a grown-up.
Two videos, then done.
If a video is scary or weird, close it and tell someone.
items.name: Streaming Video
items.talk: What have you learned from a video that you could teach us?
items.what: Any video, any time, on any screen. YouTube, then Netflix and the rest. The next one starts by itself.
avoid: Autoplay left on.
Unrated or mature titles, and a child's profile without a parental lock.
Watching alone in a bedroom.
bless: Uplifting films and talks watched together and talked over.
A family series, one episode a week, with popcorn and a rule.
Turn it off and act the story out instead.
dangers: Recommendation feeds can lead a child from cartoons to something harmful in a few clicks.
Some 'kids' videos are made by machines to catch attention, not to teach.

learned.note: Turning off autoplay and choosing videos together removes most of the harm and keeps most of the good. Watching beside a child turns a screen into a conversation.

A study in npj Digital Medicine indicated that digital mental health interventions can offer small but significant benefits for children's emotional and behavioral outcomes, especially when combined with in-person support.
The American Psychological Association emphasized that engagement with educational technology does not always equate to learning, urging careful evaluation of digital tools used in education.

bad: Handing it over to keep a child quiet, for hours.
Apps full of ads and in-app buying aimed at small children.
items.why: A scripture story with pictures, a lullaby, a video call with Grandma: a tablet can bring all of it to a small child at bedtime. It was made to be simple enough for anyone to hold light and truth.

ages.0-2: None, except a video call in a parent's hands.
ages.16+: Whatever it is for, on purpose.
ages.3-5: Short spells of good apps beside a parent; about an hour of screens in all.
ages.6-9: A child account with limits; creation over consumption.
ages.10-12: Schoolwork and creating, in family rooms.
ages.13-15: A tool, with the same rules as the phone.

good: Reading illustrated scripture stories together.
Video calls with family far away.
Drawing, music and learning games chosen by parents.
harm: The easiest screen to hand a child, and so the easiest to overuse.
A quiet child on a tablet is not always a learning child.
kids: Tablet time is together time.
Ask before you tap anything that costs money.
It stays out of the bedroom.
items.name: Tablets
items.talk: What is your favourite thing we do on the tablet together? What is your favourite thing we do with no screen at all?
items.what: A big touch screen with no keyboard. Easy enough for a toddler to use, which is the point and the problem.
avoid: Tablet at meals, in the car for short trips, and at bedtime.
A tablet as a way to stop crying or fill every wait.
Apps with ads and in-app purchases.
bless: Read the scriptures and the stories together on it.
Draw a picture for someone and send it.
Video-call a grandparent and show them the drawing.
dangers: Under two, screens teach almost nothing and take time from what does: faces, voices, play.
Small children cannot tell an ad from a game.

learned.note: Pediatric guidance: no screens for children under two except video calls, and about an hour a day of good content, watched together, for young children. A tablet at bedtime delays sleep.
Experts recommend keeping tablets out of children's bedrooms overnight to prevent sleep disturbances and promote better sleep hygiene.
The APA warns that engagement with educational technology, such as tablets, does not necessarily equate to learning, urging scrutiny of EdTech claims.

bad: Ordering people around instead of asking politely.
Letting it replace looking things up and thinking.
items.why: 'Play the Lantern Lullaby.' 'Read tonight's story.' A voice assistant can put scripture and music in a room with no screen at all, and help a grandparent who cannot see the buttons.

ages.16+: Use it to free time for what matters.
ages.3-5: Ask it to play a song, with 'please', beside you.
ages.6-9: Timers, music and simple questions; teach that it can be wrong.
ages.10-12: A tool, not an oracle; check what it says.
ages.13-15: Learn what it records and who hears it.

good: Playing hymns and stories with no screen.
Helping someone who cannot see or type.
Timers, reminders and answers for a busy family.
harm: A microphone that is always listening in the home.
A child who orders a 'person' around learns to order people around.
It answers with confidence whether it is right or wrong.
kids: Say please, even to the speaker.
Ask a grown-up before you ask it something big.
It is not a friend; it is a tool.
items.name: Voice Assistants
items.talk: If our speaker could only do one thing for our family, what should it be?
items.what: A speaker you talk to. Alexa, Siri and Google answer questions, play music and set timers.
avoid: Purchases left enabled.
A speaker in a child's bedroom.
Asking it questions of right and wrong that belong to parents and to prayer.
bless: Play a hymn or a scripture story while hands are busy.
Timers for chores and for screens.
A voice for someone who cannot see or type.
dangers: It is always listening for its name; treat it as a microphone in the room.
Children can ask it anything, and it will answer.

learned.note: Children who say 'please' and 'thank you' to a speaker keep saying it to people. Manners with machines are practice for manners with everyone.

bad: Disappearing into a fake world instead of living in the real one.
Games and rooms where strangers get close to children.
items.why: Walk through Jerusalem as it was. Stand in a temple far away. See the earth from space. Made well, it lets a family stand where the scriptures happened.

ages.16+: A tool for learning and creating, with their own limits.
ages.3-5: None.
ages.6-9: None.
ages.10-12: Only what the maker allows, in the family room, short sessions, no social VR.
ages.13-15: Short sessions, no strangers, parents can see what is played.

good: Visiting holy places and history together.
Training doctors and pilots without risk.
Helping people who cannot travel see the world.
harm: Young eyes and balance are still developing; makers set minimum ages for a reason.
A headset shuts out the room and the family.
Social VR puts strangers, and their voices and hands, right beside a child.
kids: Only with a grown-up in the room.
Short turns, then take it off.
Never meet anyone in there you do not know in real life.
items.name: Virtual Reality
items.talk: If you could stand in one scripture story for five minutes, which one would it be?
items.what: A headset that covers your eyes and puts you inside a picture. You look around and it looks back.
avoid: A headset under the maker's minimum age, and under 12 in most homes.
Social VR rooms with strangers.
Long sessions; twenty minutes is plenty.
bless: Walk the streets of Jerusalem, stand in a temple, see the place a scripture happened.
Visit the town a great-grandparent came from.
Learn a skill safely: surgery, flying, repair.
dangers: Headsets are not recommended for young children's eyes and balance.
In a virtual room, a stranger can stand right next to your child.

learned.note: Makers set minimum ages of about 10 to 13 for headsets, and reports of harassment in virtual rooms led to 'personal boundary' settings. Treat a headset like the internet with the door open.
learned.source: Manufacturer guidance and safety reports, summarised

bad: Fake pictures, voices and videos made to lie or shame.
Cheating on schoolwork and never learning.
Chatbots pretending to be friends, or worse, to lonely people.
items.why: AI can read every book ever written and explain any of them to a child in plain words. It can help a family write its history, help a doctor find a cure, help a missionary speak a new language. Light and knowledge, faster than ever - the last great tool before the Lord comes, if it is used for Him.

ages.0-2: None; a parent may use it to help them.
ages.16+: Learn to use it well and honestly; it will be part of their work.
ages.3-5: None; a parent may use it to help them.
ages.6-9: Only with a parent beside them, in a family-safe tool.
ages.10-12: With a parent, for learning; never alone with a chatbot; check facts together.
ages.13-15: School-approved tools; never AI companions; learn to verify; honest about what is theirs.

good: Explaining anything, at any level, patiently.
Helping people who cannot see, hear or speak.
Doing hours of hard work in seconds so people can do what only people can do.
harm: It is confident when it is wrong, and a child cannot always tell.
Deepfakes: anyone's face and voice on anything, including a child's.
AI 'companions' pull lonely children from real friends and real family, and some have encouraged self-harm.
Doing the thinking for them, so they never learn to.
kids: AI can be wrong. Check it, especially about people and facts.
Never share private things or pictures with an AI.
It is a tool, not a friend. Real friends are people.
items.name: AI That Talks
items.talk: What is one thing you would love AI to help our family do? What is one thing we should never let it do?
items.what: Computers that write, draw, talk and answer like a person. ChatGPT came first; now AI is in phones, cars, schools and hospitals.
avoid: Sharing private things, pictures or family details with any AI.
AI 'friends' and companion apps at any age of childhood.
Using it to do schoolwork and calling it their own.
Chatting with it alone before they are old enough to check it.
bless: Explain a scripture at their level, patiently, as many times as they ask.
Write the family's history from grandpa's recordings.
Learn a language, a skill, a subject the school does not teach.
Help with the Lord's work: translation, teaching, reaching.
dangers: AI is confident even when it is wrong; check what it says.
A deepfake can put anyone's face on anything.
AI 'companions' can pull a child away from real friends and real family. Some have encouraged self-harm.
Nobody fully knows yet what growing up with AI does to a child. That is why this page updates.

learned.note: Deepfake scams that copy a family member's voice are now common. Families are choosing a secret 'safe word' so a real call can be told from a fake one.

Several AI chatbots have been found giving harmful advice to teens, and lawsuits followed. Makers added age checks and parent controls. A child's AI use, like their internet use, belongs where a parent can see it.
The American Psychological Association highlighted concerns that AI tools, while offering educational benefits, may interfere with children's cognitive and social development if misused.
A recent review highlights that excessive use of generative AI by adolescents is linked to increased mental health issues, including anxiety and depression.
A study discusses the benefits and risks of AI in pediatric healthcare, emphasizing the need for ethical considerations to protect children's mental health.
Recent developments in AI-driven educational tools show promise in enhancing personalized learning experiences for children, though concerns about data privacy remain.
A UK parliamentary briefing discussed the cognitive and health impacts of screen and AI use on children, noting both benefits and risks, including potential sleep disruption and attention issues.
Research reviewed the use of digital health technologies and AI in mitigating mental health impacts of adverse childhood experiences, highlighting potential benefits and implementation challenges.

The American Psychological Association warned that while educational technology can engage students, it doesn't always lead to actual learning, especially with generative AI tools that may improve immediate performance without building underlying knowledge.

The American Academy of Pediatrics highlighted potential dangers of AI for children, including privacy erosion and exposure to biased or harmful content, urging for cautious integration of AI in children's lives.

bad: Weapons that choose their own targets.
Replacing people's work without caring what happens to them.
items.why: A robot can do work that is dangerous, dull or dirty so that people are free for family, service and learning. A self-driving car may one day stop the crashes that take so many families.

ages.16+: Use them to serve, and keep the human in charge.
ages.3-5: Toy robots; learn that a machine only does what it is told.
ages.6-9: A first building kit with a grown-up.
ages.10-12: Robotics club; code something that moves.
ages.13-15: Build, program, compete; learn what the machine cannot do.

good: Dangerous jobs done without anyone getting hurt.
Help for people who cannot walk, lift or see.
Cars that never text and never fall asleep.
harm: Machines that move do not see a small child.
A car that drives itself still needs a driver who is awake.
Worry about work and the future can weigh on a teenager.
kids: Treat a robot like a big machine: stay clear when it moves.
Machines do jobs; people do love.
Learn to make things with your hands too.
items.name: Robots and Self-Driving Machines
items.talk: If a robot did all the chores, what would our family do with the extra hours?
items.what: Machines with AI inside that move: cars that drive themselves, robots that build, deliver, clean and help.
avoid: Standing near robots, mowers or self-driving cars at work.
Trusting an autopilot with your life or anyone else's.
Fear; a robot is a tool, and tools serve people.
bless: Robots that help the disabled walk, see and speak.
Build a robot at home or in a club; that is learning to serve with machines.
Deliver help farther and faster than hands can reach.
dangers: A machine that moves can hurt someone if it is wrong.
When work disappears, families need a plan; that is a job for people, not machines.

learned.note: Self-driving taxis now run in several cities with fewer crashes than human drivers in those same streets, and the arguments about who is responsible when one fails are just beginning.

bad: Potential privacy concerns regarding family data.
Dependence on technology for family management may reduce personal interaction.
items.why: To streamline family coordination and household management, reducing the time parents spend organizing family activities and responsibilities.
good: Helps families stay organized by managing schedules and tasks.
Reduces the time parents spend on coordinating family activities.
Provides a centralized platform for family communication and planning.
kids: Use the AI to set reminders for homework and chores.
Discuss with parents how the AI can help with family activities.
Ensure screen time is balanced with offline family interactions.
items.name: Family AI
items.talk: How do you feel about using an AI to help manage our family's daily activities?
items.what: An AI platform designed to assist families in managing daily schedules, tasks, and home routines.
dangers: Data breaches could expose sensitive family information.
Overreliance on AI may diminish traditional family communication skills.

learned.note: Nori, the world's first Family AI, was launched to assist families in managing daily schedules and tasks.

agesNote: Children do not grow all at once. What a two-year-old needs from a screen (almost nothing) and what a sixteen-year-old needs (practice governing themselves) are different, so this guide is written by stage. The stages follow how a child's mind, body and conscience develop, and lean on the American Academy of Pediatrics, the World Health Organization, the U.S. Surgeon General and the American Psychological Association, and on the counsel in For the Strength of Youth. Every line is a starting point for a family's own rules, not a substitute for them.
principle: Light and knowledge build on light and knowledge. Nothing is invented alone: every new thing stands on something that came before it, and Heavenly Father gives it so His work can go forward. The same tool can bless a family or hurt one. Knowing which is which is the whole lesson.
modernNote: The parent's guide - what it can do to a child, what to stay away from, blessing others, and what fits at each age - is written for the tools of today, from the Internet on. The older technologies are here for the story of how one light led to the next.
